title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
claim: A single complex-valued filter has a pole whose learnable parameters set its decay, oscillation and bandwidth, giving tunable band-pass behavior.
layout: 5 panels: top row of three boxes, bottom row of two plots; notation box
description: A five-panel figure that introduces the Recursive Quadrature Filter. The top row has three boxed panels. Panel (a) is a complex-plane plot of a purple inward spiral, the free response of y(t), with the labels input drive z(t) and filtered state y(t). Panel (b) is an s-plane sketch with a shaded stable region (Re λ < 0) and a marked pole at -α + iω0. Panel (c) is a Notation box with the governing ODE, the transfer function H(s) and definitions of τ, ω, γ, τ0, ω0, α and λ. The bottom row has two plots. Panel (d) shows the impulse response, with blue real and pink imaginary oscillations inside a dashed decaying envelope. Panel (e) shows frequency-response curves on a log axis for γ from 0.02 to 0.35, going from a sharp spike to a broad band. The palette is purple, blue and pink on white.
caption: The Recursive Quadrature Filter (RQF): pole, impulse response, and frequency response. An RQF is a scalar complex-valued temporal filter with learnable phase-prior frequency $\omega$ and bandwidth parameter $\gamma$ at a fixed base time constant $\tau$, governed by Eq. [ref]. The derived quantities are the decay rate $\alpha = \gamma/\tau$, resonant frequency $\omega_0 = (1-\gamma)\omega$, effective time constant $\tau_0 = \tau/\gamma$, and pole $\lambda = -\alpha + \iota\omega_0$. (a) Free response of $y$ in the complex plane, $y(t) = y(0)\,e^{\lambda t}$. (b) The pole lies in the stable region $\Real(\lambda) < 0$ for any $\gamma \in (0, 1)$. (c) Notation used throughout the paper. (d) Impulse response $y(t) = \alpha\,e^{\lambda t}$ to a Dirac drive $z(t) = \delta(t)$, a quadrature pair (i.e., with nearly equal amplitude responses and a nearly $90^\circ$ phase shift) oscillating inside the envelope $|y(t)| = \alpha\,e^{-t/\tau_0}$ ($\gamma = 0.1$, $\omega\tau = 0.65$). (e) Frequency response amplitude for several values of $\gamma$, from sharp resonance to broad passband.
abstract: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We compensate for this delay by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective, and we develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated temporal band-pass filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs). Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the performance of RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN with built-in attentional modulation and recurrent normalization) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, the prospective variants of these models match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF achieves 83.36% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. We also introduce selective RQFs (sRQFs), which make each filter's input gain and, optionally, its bandwidth and tuning frequency input-dependent while retaining the parallel scan. With the input gain alone, the same six-layer model achieves 86.31% on Path-X; with all three input-dependent, a four-layer prospective sRQF solves Selective Copying (99.83%).
